Note the earlier WORLD_RESULTS entry read the wrong chapter of this file (Tryon 2010 on Espiritu Santo).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Accent (Schütz's term: a combination of pitch, duration and loudness) falls on every syllable with a long vowel or a diphthong (on the first element of the diphthong, wherever it sits), and otherwise on the penult of a 'measure' (accent unit) of light syllables. Words and phrases are strings of 1-3-syllable measures: an even measure is an accented heavy/superheavy syllable or a light disyllable accented on its first syllable; an uneven measure is an even measure preceded by one unaccented light syllable. The last measure of the word (or phrase) carries the main accent, so in isolation main stress is final if the final syllable is heavy and otherwise penultimate (Hayes's rules a and b are endorsed, p.406). In longer all-light words the measure divisions follow the morphemes (makùahíne, pùlelehúa, hònekakála), not right-to-left alternation.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Primary vs secondary accent is a feature of the phonological phrase: 'the last measure in the word (phrase) is emphasised to mark its end'; the peaks of earlier measures are the 'secondary accents', marked 'only for the compiler convenience' (p.407 n.3). The alternating-syllable secondary-stress rule of Pukui & Elbert 1961 (p.xxix) and Hayes 1995 is explicitly rejected (p.406-407): sequences of a light disyllable plus trisyllable (pùlelehúa, hònekakála, makùahíne) produce two adjacent light syllables. Light function words (ka, he, ʻo, i) have no intrinsic accent and take it from their position in the measure, e.g. [wahíne] but [kà wa][híne] (p.415).
new_statements.exceptions: Light monosyllabic suffixes (-na NR, -la EMPH, -a, -hi, -ki, -ʻi, -i) shift the accent one syllable right: móe > moé-na 'mat', áku > akúla; 'These suffixes change the accent of the base form only when the preceding syllables are short.. If the base form ends in a long vowel or a diphthong, it retains its accent' (p.414); 'Prefixes and markers that precede a content morpheme never change its accent pattern' (p.414). Resyllabification across morphemes creates diphthongs (ʻo ia > ʻóia, ma uka > máuka). Schütz characterises Hawaiian accent as 'neither regular nor contrastive (i.e. neither predictable nor phonemic), but demarcative' (p.408), and says there are 'no exceptional forms' once even/uneven measures are combined freely (p.414).
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe Hawaiian in general (no dialect-specific stress claim). Schütz 2010's data are formal read speech from the Hawaiian Sentence Book tape (Snakenberg 1988); Kettig 2021's corpus is archival recordings of non-Niʻihau 'Type-1' native speakers, and its stress section is a summary of Schütz 1981/2010 rather than new data. Schütz 2010 uses 'accent' (pitch + duration + loudness) deliberately instead of 'stress'.

new_statements.quote: [pp.65-66] In the case of content words comprising a single measure and thus containing a single stressed syllable, the assignment of stress is predictable from the word shape alone. Stress falls on the final syllable if the final syllable contains a diphthong or a long vowel; otherwise, stress falls on the penultimate syllable. [p.66] Primary stress falls on the stressed syllable in the final measure, while secondary stress falls on all other stressed syllables: /ˌma.ke.ˈma.ke/. [pp.66-67] However, in words of greater than four syllables, it becomes difficult to predict stress without a knowledge of the morphemes that comprise such words.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Following Schütz 1981/2010: within a measure, stress is final if the final syllable has a long vowel or diphthong, otherwise penultimate; longer words are sequences of measures, with primary stress on the final measure and secondary stress on the stressed syllables of the other measures (/ˌma.ke.ˈma.ke/ makemake). Word-final diphthongs and long vowels always carry primary stress; diphthongs and long vowels elsewhere carry secondary stress; word-final short vowels are never stressed; a short vowel next to a heavy syllable is unstressed; a short vowel is stressed if it directly precedes an unstressed syllable in the same word. Beyond four syllables the measure parse depends on the morphemes (ʻelemakule [ˌʔe.le.ma.ˈku.le] vs makuahine [ma.ˌku.a.ˈhi.ne]).
new_statements.secondary_stress: 'Primary stress falls on the stressed syllable in the final measure, while secondary stress falls on all other stressed syllables' (p.66); 'all diphthongs and long vowels that occur word-finally will by definition have primary stress, while all diphthongs and long vowels that occur elsewhere in a word will have secondary stress' (p.66).
new_statements.exceptions: Words of more than four syllables require morpheme knowledge (ʻelemakule vs makuahine, p.67); names that orthographically unite a noun phrase, e.g. Hiʻiakaikapoliopele, where function-word i does not form an /ai/ diphthong with aka (p.67); Kainoa [ˌkai.ˈno.a] may merge measures into a diphthong (p.67 n.4). Function words with a single short vowel cannot stand alone as measures and attach to the left edge of a content-word measure (p.65).

sources.quote: p.406: of Hayes's Fijian-type rules '(a) If the final syllable is light, main stress falls on the penult. (b) If the final syllable is heavy, main stress falls on the final syllable. (c) Secondary stress falls on remaining heavy syllables, and on every other light syllable...' Schütz says 'statements (a), (b), and the first half of (c) are valid. The incorrect portion is the phrase in (c) referring to alternating syllables' (pùlelehúa, makùahíne vs ‘èlemakúle). fn.3: 'the last measure in the word (phrase) is emphasised to mark its end'. p.409: within a measure 'Accent occurs on: 1. a syllable
sources.locator: pp.406-407 (sec. 2), fn.3 p.407, p.409 (three accent principles, even/uneven measures, Table 1)
sources.note: The Hawaiian accent specialist's fullest statement; explicitly validates final-heavy-else-penult primary stress and all-heavy secondary stress while rejecting alternating light-syllable secondary stress — exactly the hedge our 'weight-hedged' coding encodes. downloaded now; should be added to the record's sources.
